ingredients.item: Korean radish or daikon, peeled, cut into 2.5 cm cubes

instructions.heading: Step 1
instructions.action: The drained cubes and the paste folded together with your hands until every cube wears a coat and the bowl runs deep red-orange.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: taste a pasted cube raw: salty, savory-hot, the radish's sweet pepper under it. This is day zero — the flavor that ferments into the bowl.

instructions.heading: Step 2
instructions.action: Pack into a clean jar with 3 cm of headspace, pressed to squeeze out air, weight on top, loose lid — B01's entire packing law, unchanged.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: brine rises over the cubes within a day (top up with the saved brine or salted water if it lags — under-liquid is the safety architecture, same as the cabbage).

instructions.heading: Step 3
instructions.action: Ferment at cool room temperature 1–2 days (radish runs faster than cabbage — its sugars are more available) until the brine fizzes faintly and the sourness arrives, then refrigerate.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: day-two taste: the cube snaps audibly, the paste's heat has rounded, a clean sour line on the finish. Kkakdugi's window from young-crunchy to complex-sour is weeks in the fridge, and its snap outlives cabbage's by a wide margin.

storageNotes: Refrigerated, honestly good a month — radish's crunch holds longer than cabbage's. The brine keeps serving (see Note) until the jar is empty.
Variations: the cabbage parent (#B01); cubed Asian pear folded in at packing (the palace style, sweet bursts); the same paste on cucumber runs #B03 at its faster clock.
